:::{#thm-pd-inverse}
#### A positive definite matrix has a positive definite inverse

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ positive definite matrix
(@def-positive-definite) with real entries,
with eigendecomposition $\matr{A} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}$
(@def-eigendecomposition)
and eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_p$.
Then $\matr{A}$ is invertible (@def-invertible-matrix),

$$
\matr{A}^{-1} = \matr{Q}\,\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\,\tp{\matr{Q}},
\qquad
\matr{\Lambda}^{-1} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1/\lambda_1 & \cdots & 0           \\
\vdots      & \ddots & \vdots      \\
0           & \cdots & 1/\lambda_p
\end{bmatrix},
$$

and $\matr{A}^{-1}$ is positive definite.

:::

::: proof

By @thm-definite-eigenvalues, every $\lambda_i > 0$,
so $\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}$ is well defined,
and multiplying the two diagonal matrices entry by entry
gives $\matr{\Lambda}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1} = \matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\matr{\Lambda} = \matr{I}_p$.
Write $\matr{B} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\tp{\matr{Q}}$. Then:

$$
\ba
\matr{A}\matr{B}
&= \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\matr{I}_p\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(} \tp{\matr{Q}}\matr{Q} = \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(identity matrix)}
\\
&= \matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}}
&& \text{(} \matr{\Lambda}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1} = \matr{I}_p \text{)}
\\
&= \matr{I}_p
&& \text{(} \matr{Q} \text{ is orthogonal)}
\ea
$$

The same steps, with $\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}$ and $\matr{\Lambda}$ swapped,
give $\matr{B}\matr{A} = \matr{I}_p$,
so $\matr{B} = \matr{A}^{-1}$ (@def-matrix-inverse).
The steps with $\matr{Q}$ use @def-orthogonal-matrix,
whose remark records that $\matr{Q}\tp{\matr{Q}} = \matr{I}_p$ too,
and the identity step uses @thm-identity.

$\matr{A}^{-1}$ is symmetric by @cor-inverse-symmetric.
For $\vx \neq \vzero$, let $\vecf{y} = \tp{\matr{Q}}\vx$,
which is not $\vzero$ because $\vx = \matr{Q}\vecf{y}$.
As in the proof of @thm-definite-eigenvalues:

$$
\ba
\tp{\vx}\matr{A}^{-1}\vx
&= \tp{\vecf{y}}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\vecf{y}
&& \text{(substitute } \matr{A}^{-1} = \matr{Q}\matr{\Lambda}^{-1}\tp{\matr{Q}} \text{)}
\\
&= \sumip \frac{y_i^2}{\lambda_i}
&& \text{(} \matr{\Lambda}^{-1} \text{ is diagonal)}
\\
&> 0
&& \text{(each } \lambda_i > 0 \text{, and some } y_i \neq 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

So $\matr{A}^{-1}$ is positive definite.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-pd-inverse}
#### Inverting a positive definite matrix

For $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$,
@exm-spectral gives
$\matr{Q} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$
and eigenvalues $3$ and $1$, so:

$$
\ba
\matr{A}^{-1}
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute; } \matr{Q} \text{ is symmetric)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 1 \\ 1/3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply the first two matrices)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 4/3 & -2/3 \\ -2/3 & 4/3 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{3} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(simplify)}
\ea
$$

Multiplying out,
$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \cd \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
= \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \matr{I}_2$.

:::
